asr.full_text: Luka Panević Reviewer 05.04.01 In five minutes or less, I'm gonna try and present to you a case for why everyone in this room should start a Bitcoin company. But before you do that, why don't we start with what the heck is Bitcoin? Bitcoin was invented 7 years ago by an individual named Satoshi Nakamoto, and people don't know who this individual's identity is. People think that it's actually a group of very brilliant libertarian cryptographer somewhere but what Bitcoin essentially did was it removed the need for a financial intermediary to transact value so I could send you a hundred dollars instantly securely with zero fees using the Bitcoin protocol and network now despite amazing potential, a lot of people have come out and said that actually this has no value and no long-term sort of need. Jamie Dimon, the CEO of JP Morgan famous dismissed it as a fad and a number of others have claimed its death at least 40 times as early as January of this year. And the reason they say that is because they think of Bitcoin as digital currency. When you look at the price of Bitcoin, in late 2013, the price of Bitcoin went, actually increased by tenfold, in only a span of a month. It made a ton of people rich, but since then, over the last couple of years, the price of Bitcoin has declined by over 80%, which is why people say it's a bubble, it's irrelevant, it has no long-term use, but over that same period of time when you look at usage adoption in terms of the number of transactions on the Bitcoin network, that same story is not true actually. The number of transactions has increased by 150% over that same exact time period. So what's going on? Early-stage venture investments in 2012 into Bitcoin and blockchain-related companies was a mere $2 million. I mean, you can probably pull it out of your wallet or something right now. But. It's probably true. Let's be honest, let's be honest. But that has increased to $350 million last year, and this year, by the end, it's expected to reach a billion. It is one of the fastest and hottest growing areas of not only fintech, but also technology in general. And the reason for that is because people are starting to realize that it's actually capable of solving real problems, not only for people but for economies. Let me give you an example. A Filipino house worker that lives in the Philippines moves to Hong Kong to provide for their family. They remit money, 50 US dollars a week or something like that, and they use companies like Western Union and Monegram and for each of those transactions, they are incurring anywhere from 10 to 40% fees. That is crazy and that is killing, you know, their livelihoods. So, what companies have done, startups have done, have come in to use the Bitcoin Protocol Network to provide the exact same service for up to a tenth of the cost. These two companies were actually started or founded or led by Haas MBAs, and this is something that we should all be, as a community, very proud about. But this is real value to the customer, real value to people in the world. And so what started out as a P2P network between individuals is now starting to be explored by people across the entire ecosystem. Businesses for Supply Chain payments, governments for, welfare distribution, banks for court infrastructure and NGOs for releasing foreign aid. And what has happened more recently, in the past couple months that big players have to started to step in. Jamie Dimon, actually, a couple of weeks ago wrote to his annual shareholders list and said that maybe he got it wrong. Now one of the biggest Bitcoin supporters is Marc Andreessen, and he wrote in 2014 about how we can reinvent the entire thing with Bitcoin. And that thing that he is referring to is the entire financial system. Companies across the board are starting to build out the core infrastructure to design a new financial system that hasn't fundamentally changed in the last 200 more years. And so one of the interesting things that's come out of this, it's actually opened and expanded people's minds. Is it possible to code into Bitcoin, the block chain, the Bitcoin network. Things other than just currency. And that's what companies across the board have started to explore outside of even financial services. One of which is the Internet of Things. Because when you think about the Internet of Things it's a machine transacting with another machine, which therefore means a payment, which therefore means a payment protocol that these machines can actually use. And people are starting to explore the use of Bitcoin in the case of the Internet of Things, which hasn't taken off for over a decade. And so, what I want to leave you with is this, an analogy, actually. If you were to ask people, what is the internet in the early 1990s? people would actually really struggle to tell you what it is. Some people would say, that's a French technology that's going to go away. Some people might say, it's actually a means for sending, receiving and storing information. Some people might say that it's a platform for communication and yet, some others, maybe back then would say that it's a protocol for building applications, new services, new businesses that people can't even imagine yet. So my question is, what is Bitcoin? Is it the digital coin that people think about in the news? Or is it something much bigger? Is it a protocol on which new things can be built? Is it the HTTP of financial services? Thank you very much!
